# Prescriptive lessons -- brent-greenan x jazz-standards-playbook

## maj7

Greenan treats maj7 exclusively as the tonic resolution point of the ii-V-I: its 3rd and 7th are the guide-tone targets that voice-lead to and from the surrounding dominant, and Ionian is its default pitch collection in any Note Choice Map. One variant function appears -- the bIImaj7 as tritone-substitution V-chord replacement -- where the major quality is what distinguishes it from a standard dominant tritone sub and must be preserved analytically.

- [ch.2] Maj7 is the tonic chord of the Major Diatonic Series and the resolution point of the ii-V-I. Formula: Root-3-5-7. The 3rd and 7th are defining guide tones and primary melodic targets.
- [ch.4] "Continue to let the 3rds and 7ths of each chord be your guide." The guide-tone rule is restated as the governing principle for improvising over any maj7: the 3rd and 7th anchor all melodic decisions, and chord tones (Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th) extend the inventory.
- [ch.8] Moving from Cmaj7 to Cmin7, only b3 and b7 require adjustment -- all other tones hold. The maj7 functions here as the stable reference against which the minor-quality adjustments are measured.
- [ch.8] The bIImaj7 substitutes for the V chord in a ii-V-I: "The easiest way to think of this chord is a substitute for the V chord." Its major quality -- not dominant -- is analytically load-bearing; the student must not re-analyze it as a standard tritone sub dom7.
- [ch.11] The Note Choice Map assigns Ionian (1-2-3-4-5-6-7) over every maj7 functioning as tonic. EbMAJ7 -> Ionian, BbMAJ7 -> Ionian. This confirms Ionian as the unambiguous default; no other scale is prescribed for unaltered tonic maj7 chords.

## min7

Greenan's min7 teaching pivots on context: in functional progressions it is the ii chord with guide-tone voice-leading duties; in modal contexts (So What) guide-tone technique is explicitly suspended and Dorian serves as a static pitch collection. A third axis -- the diatonic vi minor raised to VI7 -- signals that minor quality on any diatonic chord is provisional and should be treated as a dominant-conversion candidate.

- [ch.2] Min7 is the ii chord of the ii-V-I: formula Root-b3-5-b7; its 3rd and 7th are guide tones that resolve stepwise to the 3rd of the V7. There is "no more important chord progression to know than the ii-V-I."
- [ch.2 / ch.6] Diatonic minor chords -- especially vi -- can and should be converted to dominant 7ths in jazz contexts. "It is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in the diatonic series into dominant 7th chords." The vi minor is the primary conversion target, generating VI7 secondary-dominant chains.
- [ch.4] **Proscriptive.** Over any chord with minor quality: "Don't be playing major thirds or major 7ths!" Natural 3 and natural 7 are excluded. The student must track chord quality before selecting any note.
- [ch.5] The min7 in iv position (borrowed from parallel minor) is the primary minor-iv pivot. Concrete voicing sequence: Abmin6 first, Abmin7-Db7 second, bare Db7 third. The min7 reading is the starting point before expansion.
- [ch.7] **Modal context.** Dorian (1-2-b3-4-5-6-b7) is the prescribed pitch collection when min7 is a modal tonic (D Dorian and Eb Dorian for "So What"). Treat it as a "note choice" inventory, not a fingering pattern.
- [ch.7] **Proscriptive, modal.** "Because So What is based on modal harmony, there is no need to identify the guide tones." Guide-tone technique is suspended entirely when harmonic movement is absent; diatonic arpeggios connected by nearest chord tone replace it.
- [ch.10] Generalized expansion rule: "Where there is a V chord, you can almost always add a ii in front of it." Any min7 can be prepended to its companion dom7 to convert a V-I into a ii-V-I; the student should deploy this expansion actively.
- [ch.11] The backdoor ii-V places a min7 before the bVII7: "Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7." This min7 belongs to the backdoor key area, not to the parent key -- dual-key awareness is required.

## dom7

Greenan's dom7 doctrine is built on three non-negotiable pillars: guide-tone voice-leading (7th resolves to 3rd of next chord), Mixolydian as the universal default pitch collection, and the V chord as the modulatory fulcrum at every tonal seam. Secondary dominants, VI7 conversions, backdoor dominants, and chromatic descending approaches are all variations on the same functional logic; the student applies identical guide-tone and Mixolydian tools to each.

- [ch.2] V is "always dominant" in both major and minor diatonic series. Formula: Root-3-5-b7. Guide-tone rule: "The 7th of each chord resolves to the 3rd of the next chord." This is the load-bearing voice-leading mechanism for the entire book.
- [ch.4] Secondary dominants are "dominant 7 chords that act as a V chord of a diatonic chord other than the tonic" (tonicization). Any dom7 outside primary V function targets the chord a fourth above it; guide-tone and chord-tone tools apply without modification.
- [ch.2 / ch.6] VI7 conversion: the diatonic vi minor raised to dominant generates cycling-fourths dominant chains. In "Sweet Georgia Brown," "bars 1-13 are just a long cycle of dominant 7th chords resolving to the I chord." The student should treat this conversion as idiomatic and unremarkable.
- [ch.6] Mixolydian (1-2-3-4-5-6-b7) is "the primary melodic resource over dominant 7 chords." Use it as a pitch collection -- not a scale to run in order.
- [ch.6] Chord-tone arpeggio pattern over cycling dom7 chords: ascending R-3-5-b7, then descending R-b7-5-3, each bar starting on a different chord tone. This drill ensures the student can enter the arpeggio from any position.
- [ch.6] Chromatic descending dominant approach: "a series of chromatically descending dominant 7th chords targeting the VI7 chord." Recognize this as directed approach motion toward a specific resolution target, not random chromaticism.
- [ch.6] **Proscriptive.** "The best way to think about the use of scales is 'pitch collections.' They aren't notes that are meant to be played in order." Mixolydian over dom7 is a note-choice map; running it as a fingering pattern is explicitly warned against.
- [ch.10] The V7 is "your secret weapon for resolving to a new key center." At every tonal seam in multi-key standards, identify or insert the V7 and use it as the modulatory fulcrum.
- [ch.11] Backdoor dominant: bVII7 substitutes for V7, approaching I by whole step. "The bVII7 has a lot of notes in common with an altered V7 chord." Mixolydian maps directly onto the bVII7's note content; no scale change is needed.
- [ch.11] Note Choice Map confirmation: F7, Bb7, Ab7, Eb7 in "Stella by Starlight" all map to Mixolydian in straightforward dominant function. Mixolydian = unaltered dom7, no exceptions.

## dom7b9

Greenan consistently teaches dom7b9 through the diminished substitution lens: the four upper tones of the dom7b9 are identical to a dim7 built a major third above the root, making the substitution directly ear-verifiable. Improvisation note choice defaults to the underlying dom7b9 chord tones, not to the diminished chord's independent identity.

- [ch.9] Core rule: F#dim7 as rootless D7(b9) -- "the four chord tones of F#dim7 (F#-A-C-Eb) are identical to the upper four tones of D7(b9)." The student should always identify the implied root a minor third below the dim7 to recover the underlying dom7b9.
- [ch.9] Improvisation note source: "it is being substituted for the VI7b9 chord, so any of those chord tones will serve you well." Chord tones of the underlying dom7b9 -- not just the diminished chord's own tones -- are the primary material.
- [ch.11] Altered Scale is prescribed over dom7(b9) in chromatic approach contexts (e.g., A7(b9) -> Altered in the Stella Note Choice Map). Greenan flags this as new vocabulary not seen before ch.11; the student must study it before attempting the quarter-note solo exercise.

## dom7alt

Greenan introduces altered dominant as a chapter-11 concept specific to "Stella by Starlight" -- it is not built up across earlier chapters. The Altered Scale is the sole prescribed pitch collection, paired exclusively with A7 chords functioning in altered dominant capacity throughout the form.

- [ch.11] Altered Scale is required for altered dominant contexts in Stella, flagged explicitly as new vocabulary: "the ones you haven't seen before in this book." The Note Choice Map pairs it with A7 in altered function. The student must learn the scale before the quarter-note solo exercise -- this is a hard prerequisite, not optional enrichment.

## dom7#11

Greenan introduces Lydian Dominant as the other chapter-11 newcomer alongside Altered Scale -- both are presented as essential additions to complete the Note Choice Map for Stella's chromatic harmonic landscape.

- [ch.11] Lydian Dominant is prescribed over dominant chords where #11 (raised fourth / Lydian character) is implied or explicit in the Stella analysis. Like Altered Scale, it must be learned from the Note Choice Map before attempting the quarter-note solo. No earlier chapter prepares it; the student must not assume Mixolydian covers this context.

## min7b5

Greenan insists the half-diminished chord is only intelligible relationally -- always read it through its resolution target. The dual-analysis framework (min7b5 as both the ii of a borrowed minor ii-V and the iiib5 of the parent key) is the core analytical tool. Locrian is the default Note Choice Map assignment.

- [ch.5] Min7b5 as minor ii-V-I pivot: "If we look at a Gmin7(b5) and a C7(b9) as separate chords, they are confusing. But if we look at them as resolving to an Fmin7, then we have something functional to understand." Formula: Root-b3-b5-b7. Always read through the resolution target.
- [ch.5] Dual-analysis framework: Gmin7(b5) in a ii-V of ii is simultaneously readable as "the iiib5" within the parent key alongside VI7. "A iiib5 is odd, but again, if we combine this understanding with the ii-V of ii concept everything ties together." Both readings must be held simultaneously.
- [ch.11] Locrian (1-b2-b3-4-b5-b6-b7) is assigned to every min7b5 in the Stella Note Choice Map -- Emin7(b5) -> Locrian, Amin7(b5) -> Locrian. Locrian is the unambiguous default; no alternate mode is prescribed for these chords.
- [ch.11] Hybrid ii-V-I: min7b5 borrowed from parallel minor preceding a dom7b9 that resolves to a major I. "The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major I." The minor-quality ii is the trigger signal for the surprise major resolution; the student must recognize it before choosing note material.

## dim7

Greenan's dim7 teaching rests on a single master rule -- every dim7 is a rootless altered dominant, recoverable by locating the root a minor third below -- plus a crucial secondary function as chromatic bass-line connector. The whole-half diminished scale is prescribed as the pitch collection but immediately hedged: musical reference beats theoretical verbatim execution every time.

- [ch.9] Core substitution rule: "F#dim7 chord is a substitute for the dominant VI7 chord... You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9)." The four tones of the dim7 are identical to the upper four tones of the dom7b9. Always reinterpret a dim7 as a rootless altered dominant one minor third below its root.
- [ch.9] Dual compositional function: beyond harmonic substitution, the dim7 "is also creating a chromatic passing note, in this case the bass note, to connect the I chord with the ii chord." The student must identify which role is primary -- substitution or bass-line connector -- before selecting note choices.
- [ch.9] Whole-half diminished scale (W-H-W-H-W-H-W) is the prescribed pitch collection. But: "I don't want you to play this scale verbatim when you are improvising... just playing the music rather than spending too much time getting bogged down in theory is more helpful."
- [ch.9] **Proscriptive.** Running the whole-half diminished scale mechanically is explicitly warned against. Musical ideas from reference recordings are preferred over scale execution. The prescription is the pitch collection, not the fingering sequence.
- [ch.10] Passing diminished (biii dim) is distinct from substitution diminished: "its primary job is to connect the iii chord to the ii chord chromatically" -- it is not replacing any underlying chord. The student must classify role before choosing notes.
- [ch.9] Bridge architecture of "Have You Met Miss Jones": the A-section diminished logic gives way to ii-V-Is descending in major thirds (Bb -> Gb -> D -> back). This thirds-cycle principle is shared with Coltrane Changes; recognizing it unlocks the bridge's key-center navigation.

## min6

Greenan's min6 teaching is narrow and functional: it appears only as the primary voicing for the minor iv chord borrowed from parallel minor, positioned as the first-choice option before ii-V expansion or bare dominant simplification.

- [ch.5] Abmin6 is the preferred first voicing for the iv minor function: "often times, musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord." The voicing sequence is min6 -> min7-dom7 (full ii-V) -> bare dom7 -- always start with the min6 before considering expansion or reduction.
